topic: India's pegged regime 1971-1992: peg to the pound, then to a weighted basket (NEER) of trading partners, why it was done, why it failed (1991 devaluation), and the road to floating rates via LERMS

book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook would define NEER as a formula and list India's regimes by date. The video starts from where the last one ended (the 1971 collapse), puts the 1971-92 period on a timeline and cuts it in two, then takes the dense official sentence for 1975-92 and breaks it phrase by phrase ('basket', 'major trading partners', 'weighted average'), working each phrase with assumed numbers in a table until the NEER pops out. Only after the learner has computed it does the video ask what NEER moving up or down means, then asks 'what was the purpose?' and lets the learner infer it, and finally shows the mistake and the 1991 devaluation. It ends by re-zooming the whole timeline and explaining why the next two videos come in the order floating, then LERMS.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Take one dense definition sentence, cut it into its phrases, and turn each phrase into one step of a worked calculation; then ask what the result does, why it was chosen, and why it failed.

narration.density: About 14 terms (pegged regime, pound sterling, basket of currencies, major trading partners, weighted average, weight, nominal exchange rate, NEER, appreciation, depreciation, trade deficit, misalignment, export competitiveness, BoP crisis, two-step devaluation, floating regime, LERMS) in about 7.7 minutes, about 2 per minute, several recalled. talmel_summary: The calculation half fits well: the basket of mixed notes tied by a rope to the rupee turns 'pegged to a basket' into a picture, and the table fills row by row as each weight and rate is spoken, ending in a lit answer column and the single number 0.048. The cause half drifts to text: the NEER-up/down boxes, the purpose answer, and the misalignment chain are statements stacked on screen, often several seconds before the voice. A home-base composition (strip, basket, rope, rupee) is returned to three times, which keeps the learner oriented.

voice.notes: About 187 words per minute, steady and patient. Uses invitation lines that make the learner think ('ab aap zara thande dimaag se socho', 'I am sure aap is uddeshya ko khud hi samajh pa rahe honge') before giving the answer. Phrases 'chaliye is poori statement ko breakdown karte hain' and 'yaani' mark unpacking. Small decimals are read digit by digit ('0.034', '0.048'); percentages plainly. A slight dramatic turn at 'bahut hi jaldi humein apni mistake realize hone lagi'. Ends by justifying the order of the next two videos.

game_ideas.player_does: Fills the basket: sets each partner's weight from a trade-share bar (they must add to 100%) and drags in each partner's per-rupee rate.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each row computes weight x rate in the answer column; the column sums into the NEER number, which hangs from the basket tied to the rupee note.
game_ideas.win: Reach the target NEER for the given year with weights that match the trade shares.
game_ideas.lose: Weights that do not add to 100% leave the basket lopsided and the NEER cell blank; a wrong product lights that row red.

game_ideas.player_does: Moves a NEER slider up or down and predicts what happens to the rupee and to the trade deficit before the system plays it.
game_ideas.process_happens: NEER up: the rupee note rises against the basket, exports shrink, the deficit bar grows; NEER down: the reverse.
game_ideas.win: Predict all four links correctly for both directions.
game_ideas.lose: A wrong prediction replays the chain with the mismatched link highlighted.
game_ideas.concept: NEER, appreciation/depreciation and the trade deficit

game_ideas.player_does: Runs India's exports to the US while the rupee stays pegged to the partner basket; rival exporters (China, Indonesia) can depreciate against the dollar.
game_ideas.process_happens: When a rival depreciates, its goods get cheaper on the US shelf, India's orders fall, the reserve meter drains toward a BoP crisis; the learner can hold the peg or devalue in steps.
game_ideas.win: Keep exports and reserves alive, which needs a timely two-step devaluation.
game_ideas.lose: Holding the peg too long shows India's shelf emptying and a BoP crisis banner, as in 1991.
game_ideas.concept: why the basket peg failed and led to the 1991 devaluation

game_ideas.player_does: Places regimes on a 1944-today strip: Bretton Woods (to 1971), peg to pound (1971-75), basket/NEER peg (1975-92), LERMS (1992-93), floating (1993-).
game_ideas.process_happens: The strip colours green for fixed and blue for floating as cards land, with the 1991 devaluation marker.
game_ideas.lose: Placing floating before LERMS shows the next-lesson note: LERMS needs floating explained first, but came first in time.

checks_learned: Counts said must match counts shown (the voice says 6 partner countries, the table shows 5).
A dense definition shown as a note should be followed by a phrase-by-phrase unpack, each phrase highlighted as it is explained (E05 does the unpack; the highlight is missing).
A worked calculation should show every row being computed in step with the voice; rows done 'the same way' may fill together, but the total must be spoken (E05 does this).
A cause shown only on screen (convertibility suspended, at 9.6 s) must be spoken at least once.
Long-standing condition boxes (NEER up / down) should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice starts them.
A promo overlay must never cover a recap view.
A question to the learner ('what was the purpose?') should leave a short pause before the answer appears on screen.

teaching_best.why: 'Let us break down this whole statement': the official one-line definition is unpacked phrase by phrase, each phrase becoming one step of the work.
A basket of mixed banknotes tied to the rupee note by a rope makes 'pegged to a basket' literal.
The weighted average is built in a table with assumed weights and real-looking rates, so the NEER is computed, not just defined.
'Think with a cool head' and 'I am sure you can work out the purpose yourself' make the learner infer before the answer.
Justifies the order of the next lessons (floating before LERMS) by prerequisite, not by date.

teaching_weak.why: The misalignment story (about 66 s) is stacked statements; rivals' cheaper goods and India's falling orders are never pictured.
The switch to the per-rupee format (1 rupee = 0.012 dollars) is quick and only spoken; it is the step most learners trip on.
The collapse reason appears only as an on-screen box.
The full-timeline recap is partly covered by an app promo overlay.
Both NEER boxes are long paragraphs that appear before the voice reaches them.
